title: The Tree Under Whose Shade: Badaun, Ajodhan, and the Hospice at Ghiyaspur
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Badaun, the House of the Bukhara Exiles

stops.name: Badaun, birth in the Sayyid house
stops.date_confidence: contested year: 1238 is commonest, 1237 (635 AH) is also given and Wikipedia itself notes the discrepancy, and a minority tradition gives 1244; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: The family came out of Bukhara ahead of the Mongol advance and stopped at Badaun in the Ganges plain. Here a son is born to Syed Ahmad Bukhari and Bibi Zulekha, in a house that traces its line to the Prophet and keeps the manners of a scholarship carried out of a burned country. Badaun is a sultan's town with Iltutmish's great mosque at its center, and it is where the boy learns his letters. Delhi is a hundred and fifty miles west. He will spend fifty-nine years of his life within a mile of one hut on the Yamuna, and never once go further west than the Sutlej.
suggested_refs: The Sayyid quarter of Badaun, refuge of Bukharan families displaced by the Mongol conquest of Transoxiana

stops.name: Badaun, the father's grave at the Shamsi mosque
stops.date_confidence: attested that the father dies when the boy is about five; the exact year follows from the disputed birth year and the burial site itself is tradition, not document
stops.campa: The father dies when the boy is about five. Tradition puts him in the tomb compound attached to Iltutmish's Shamsi Jama Masjid, beside the grandfather, and the family becomes what the Chishti record is full of: a widow, a son, and no income. Bibi Zulekha will be the fixed point of his life for forty years, and it is at her grave, not at any sultan's audience, that he will be found on the one day a throne demands he appear. What the boy inherits is a lineage and no means at all of living on it.
suggested_refs: The Shamsi Jama Masjid at Badaun and the tomb compound said to hold his father and grandfather

stops.name: Badaun, under Maulana Alauddin Usuli
stops.date_confidence: tradition; the pool placed this tutelage in Delhi and tagged it attested, but Usuli is consistently 'of Badayun' and thefamouspeople.com puts the schooling at Badaun before the move, so it is placed here and downgraded
stops.campa: The widow places him with the scholar Maulana Alauddin Usuli of Badayun. He takes the seven modes of Quranic recitation, Arabic grammar, hadith, tafsir, mathematics, astronomy: the full curriculum of a working alim, learned by a child with no patron. Sixty years on, ordered into a sultan's new mosque, he will answer in the register of law rather than of piety, and the answer will hold because the man making it can argue it. Wikipedia's article on him names no teacher at all.
suggested_refs: The teaching circle of Maulana Alauddin Usuli at Badaun
sources: iloveindia.com biography (which relocates this to Delhi)

stops.name: Delhi, the widow and her son arrive
stops.date_confidence: flat contradiction, unresolved: Wikipedia has the move immediately after the father's death, at age five, c. 1243; iloveindia.com dates it to 1260, when he is in his twenties and finishing hadith. Both cannot be true and the record consulted does not choose
stops.campa: Bibi Zulekha brings her son to Delhi. The city is the Qutb quarter: the minaret going up in stages, the mosque built from the stone of demolished temples, the tombs of the first Chishtis already in the ground at Mehrauli. Modern maps put medieval Delhi at Connaught Place, which was laid out in the 1930s; the older city they walk into stood here instead, around the Qutb quarter's minaret and mosque. When they arrive is disputed by six or seventeen years, depending on which biography is opened. That they arrive poor is not disputed anywhere.
suggested_refs: The Qutb complex and its teaching quarter, the Delhi of the Mamluk sultans

stops.name: Delhi, the hadith circles of the old city
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the attested fact is that he trains in Delhi's teaching circles near the Qutb quarter before moving out to Ghiyaspur, with no year fixed
stops.campa: He continues in the teaching circles clustered near the Qutb, working through hadith toward the certificate that makes a man a qadi. It is the ordinary road: study, license, appointment, salary, a judgeship in a provincial town. He is on it, and he leaves it. What turns him is not recorded in any document written while he lived. All the accounts agree only on the direction of the turn, west and north, up the Sutlej road toward a hospice kept by a man he has never met.
suggested_refs: The hadith teaching circles of thirteenth-century Delhi

stops.name: Mehrauli, the tomb of Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no primary text names such a visit. Kaki died 1 December 1235, three years before Nizam ad-Din's birth, so a tomb visit is the only possible form of contact. Year is a placeholder within his Delhi student period
stops.campa: At Mehrauli lies Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki, dead since 1235, the man Moinuddin Chishti sent to hold Delhi while he himself stayed in Rajasthan. This grave is the anchor of the Delhi line. Nizam ad-Din will inherit that line two links on, and his own grave, four miles east across the ridge, will become the anchor that replaces it. No source puts him at this stone. Every source puts his authority in descent from it, through Baba Farid, whom Kaki taught and to whom Kaki gave the succession.
suggested_refs: The dargah of Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki at Mehrauli, the anchor of the Chishti Delhi line
sources: moinuddin_chishti.journey.json, stops 'Delhi, the khirqa to Baba Farid' and 'Delhi, Mehrauli, the death of Bakhtiar Kaki'

stops.name: Ajodhan, the road to Baba Farid
stops.date_confidence: contested: Wikipedia and auqaf.punjab.gov.pk both say age twenty, which from a 1238 birth gives 1258; iloveindia.com gives 1257 outright. Month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: At twenty he goes to Ajodhan, four hundred miles up the Sutlej, where Fariduddin Ganjshakar keeps a hospice so poor that the wooden food bowls are said to be licked clean. Farid is third in the Indian Chishti line: Moinuddin to Bakhtiar Kaki to Farid. Ajodhan is not Delhi. There is no court here, no sultan, no salary, and no reason to come except the man. Farid is often counted the fourth in the chain. He is the third. Nizam ad-Din is the fourth, and he is walking toward the place where that becomes true.
suggested_refs: The Sutlej road from Delhi to Ajodhan, now Pakpattan Sharif

stops.name: Ajodhan, the oath of discipleship
stops.date_confidence: attested that the initiation happens on this first visit; the month is a placeholder. The often-repeated detail of 'seven months and some days' in the master's company is credited to auqaf.punjab.gov.pk, which on direct fetch does not contain it
stops.campa: He takes the hand of Fariduddin Ganjshakar and becomes his disciple. The chain that starts at Chisht in Khorasan, runs through Ajmer and Mehrauli, and has been in India sixty years, now has a Delhi-trained scholar in it who can hold his own in a law court. Farid keeps him some months, then sends him back east. The most commonly repeated figure for that first stay, seven months and some days, is not on the page it is usually credited to; the page was fetched, and it says only that Farid met the twenty-year-old Nizamuddin.
suggested_refs: The khanqah of Baba Farid at Ajodhan, before the shrine was built over it
sources: auqaf.punjab.gov.pk, Pakpattan shrine page (checked directly; does not carry the seven-month detail)

stops.name: Ajodhan, the Ramadan returns
stops.date_confidence: attested that he returns annually to spend Ramadan with his master and that three visits fall within Farid's lifetime; the count of ten lifetime pilgrimages, seven of them to the grave, is from auqaf.punjab.gov.pk and is tradition
stops.campa: Every year he goes back up the Sutlej to keep Ramadan beside his master. Three of these fall inside Farid's life. The shrine's own account raises the lifetime total to ten, the remaining seven made to a grave. It is a long way to walk for a month of fasting in a hospice with no food in it. He does it while other men his age take appointments, and the walking is the training, since nothing here is transmitted except in person, in the month when nobody eats.
suggested_refs: The annual Ramadan journey between Delhi and Ajodhan

stops.name: Ajodhan, the khilafat and the turban of Chisht
stops.date_confidence: the investiture is attested and its saying is quoted verbatim; the year is the commonly cited c. 1265. The rival date 2 Rabi al-Awwal 656 AH, c. 9 March 1258, is dropped as internally impossible, since it would fall on the first visit while the sources put khilafat on the third
stops.campa: On the third visit Farid confers khilafat and names him khalifa of Delhi, handing over the ceremonial turban said to have come down from Chisht itself. The words are recorded. One rival tradition dates the investiture to 656 AH, seven years earlier, which cannot stand: that date falls on the first visit, and every account puts the turban on the third. The old man is giving away a city he has never lived in, to a man who has not yet built anything in it.
stops.quote: You will be a tree under whose soothing shade people will find comfort
stops.quote_source: Fariduddin Ganjshakar to Nizam ad-Din Auliya at Ajodhan, conferring khilafat; Wikipedia, 'Nizamuddin Auliya'; sufinama.org, 'Nizamuddin Auliya: The Darwesh of Love'
suggested_refs: The Chishti khirqa and turban, transmitted Moinuddin to Kaki to Farid to Nizam ad-Din
sources: moinuddin_chishti.journey.json, stop 'Delhi, the khirqa to Baba Farid'

stops.name: Ajodhan, the master's death
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, unresolved: Wikipedia 'Baba Farid' and auqaf.punjab.gov.pk give c. 7 May 1266, aged 78; a minority chronology gives 5 Muharram 664 AH, 17 October 1265, whose conversion is sound but whose only carrier in this pool is grokipedia.com
stops.campa: Baba Farid dies at Ajodhan, aged seventy-eight, shortly after handing over the succession. The news reaches Nizam ad-Din on the Delhi road or after he arrives; the accounts differ, as they differ over whether the death falls in the autumn of 1265 or the following May. He does not stay to hold the shrine town, and he is not offered it. He was told to take Delhi, and he goes back down the Sutlej to a city where he has no house, no hospice, and no standing except a turban.
suggested_refs: The shrine of Baba Farid at Pakpattan Sharif, raised over the khanqah where the khilafat was given

segments.name: Ghiyaspur, the Voice and the Hut

stops.name: Delhi, the prayer at the Rani Reservoir
stops.date_confidence: the episode is told by Nizam ad-Din himself and recorded verbatim in Fascicle IV, Assembly 19, of 26 November 1315; the year of the event is inferred from his settlement at Ghiyaspur c. 1266, not stated in the text
stops.campa: Back in Delhi and unable to stay in it, he goes to the Rani Reservoir in the Jasrat Garden and puts the choice to God rather than to himself. A voice answers with a place name. He records, fifty years later, in his own words to a disciple holding a pen, that he had never seen Ghiyaspur and did not know where it was. It is one of the very few episodes of his life for which his own first-person account survives, and everything after it happens inside one village.
stops.quote: I must leave this city. I will not choose the place to live; the place that You choose, there will I go to live.
stops.quote_source: Fawa'id al-Fu'ad / Morals for the Heart, trans. Bruce B. Lawrence, Paulist Press 1992, Fascicle IV, Assembly 19, Wednesday 27 Sha'ban 715 AH / 26 November 1315, p. 244
suggested_refs: The Rani Reservoir in the Jasrat Garden, Delhi, site of the prayer that named Ghiyaspur
sources: Fawa'id al-Fu'ad, trans. Lawrence, p. 244 (verified against the archive.org djvu-text scan)

stops.name: Ghiyaspur, the straw roof on the Yamuna
stops.date_confidence: the settlement c. 1266 is attested; the straw-roofed hut is travel-press tradition and the month is a placeholder
stops.campa: Ghiyaspur is a hamlet on the Yamuna four miles east of the Qutb quarter, out past where the city stops. He raises a hut there and it is described as straw-roofed. Nothing in the record explains why the place answered to a prayer, and nothing needs to: he goes because he was told a name and the name turned out to exist. Delhi has a court, a mint, a minaret, and a mosque built out of temple stone. Ghiyaspur has him. Within thirty years the traffic runs the other way.
suggested_refs: The hamlet of Ghiyaspur on the Yamuna, renamed Nizamuddin after his death

stops.name: Ghiyaspur, the free kitchen
stops.date_confidence: attested in substance that the khanqah drew rich and poor alike and ran an open kitchen; the year is a placeholder inside the early khanqah period
stops.campa: The khanqah takes shape around a kitchen that does not ask who is at the door. Hindus and Muslims, nobles and laborers, come and eat, and the eating is the doctrine: there is no gate and no test. He accepts futuh, unsolicited gifts, and keeps nothing overnight. Under the Mamluk sultans, including Balban's long reign, he becomes the shaikh Delhi talks about, on the strength of a hut and a cooking fire outside the walls. No court record of that ascent survives. The evidence for it is the traffic on the road out of the city.
suggested_refs: The langar of the Ghiyaspur khanqah, open to all comers

stops.name: Ghiyaspur, Amir Khusrow enters the circle
stops.date_confidence: the relationship is attested; the year is not. Hagiography puts it at age eight, c. 1261, which is impossible since Ghiyaspur is only settled c. 1266; Wikipedia 'Amir Khusrau' says 1310 at age fifty-seven; 1272 is in fact the year of his court appointment, and is used here only as a placeholder
stops.campa: Amir Khusrow, born at Patiyali in 1253, poet in Persian and Hindavi, court servant to seven sultans, becomes the disciple whose name the world will attach to this one. When he comes is genuinely unknown: one tradition says he was a boy of eight, one source says he was fifty-seven. The master compares his two poet-disciples without softening it, and the comparison is preserved because Amir Hasan Sijzi, the sweeter rivulet in it, is the man who wrote the sentence down.
stops.quote: Our Khusrau is like a saltish river, while Hasan is like a sweetish rivulet.
stops.quote_source: Cited from Siyar al-Awliya in Khaliq Ahmad Nizami's Introduction to Morals for the Heart, Paulist Press 1992, p. 44; the onward page reference to Siyar al-Awliya could not be verified in the scan
suggested_refs: The Hindavi and Persian divans of Amir Khusrow, composed under Nizam ad-Din's direction
sources: Khaliq Ahmad Nizami, Introduction to Morals for the Heart, p. 44

stops.name: Kilokhri, a sultan builds a capital next door
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The event is historically sound, Muizuddin Qaiqabad reigning 1287 to 1290 and raising a riverside palace-city at Kilugarhi, but the pool credited it to Wikipedia 'Ghiyaspur', which on direct fetch contains no mention of Kilokhri or Qaiqabad at all
stops.campa: Sultan Muizuddin Qaiqabad founds a riverside capital at Kilokhri, a few hundred yards from the hut. For three years the saint's hamlet sits in the shadow of a new royal city. The city does not outlast its founder by much. Sultans keep arriving beside him, building, and being removed, across sixty years in which he does not move once and the throne never stops moving. The article usually cited for this connection turns out not to mention it, so it stands here as an uncited fact rather than a documented one.
suggested_refs: The palace-city of Kilugarhi on the Yamuna, raised by Muizuddin Qaiqabad beside Ghiyaspur
sources: Wikipedia, 'Ghiyaspur' (checked directly; does not support the claim)
general accounts of Muizuddin Qaiqabad's reign, 1287-1290

stops.name: Ghiyaspur, the first assembly recorded
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: the text dates this assembly 3 Sha'ban 707 AH, 27 January 1308, and Amir Hasan Sijzi records it as it happens
stops.campa: Amir Hasan Sijzi, poet and disciple, begins writing down what is said in the evening assemblies. The first dated one opens on the question of the penitent and the upright, and the master settles it in favor of the man who has ruined something and come back. The book becomes the Fawa'id al-Fu'ad, the first malfuzat of its kind in India, and it is the reason this life can be dated at all. Everything else about him is reconstruction from later hands. This is a man talking in a room, with the day written at the top of the page.
stops.quote: THE PENITENT IS EQUIVALENT TO THE UPRIGHT, since the upright is he who never drinks throughout his life or commits a single sin, while the penitent is he who has sinned and then repented of his sin. The two are equivalent, in accordance with this Tradition of the Prophet Muhammad, may peace be upon him: 'A person who repents of his sin is like someone who has never sinned.'
stops.quote_source: Fawa'id al-Fu'ad / Morals for the Heart, trans. Bruce B. Lawrence, Paulist Press 1992, Fascicle I, Assembly 1, 3 Sha'ban 707 AH / 27 January 1308, p. 81
suggested_refs: The Fawa'id al-Fu'ad, first malfuzat text of Indian Sufism, compiled 1307-1322
sources: Fawa'id al-Fu'ad, trans. Lawrence, p. 81 (verified against the archive.org djvu-text scan)

stops.name: Ghiyaspur, the fame that is forgotten
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, same assembly. The words are those of Hamid ad-din Suwali of Nagaur, quoted by Nizam ad-Din inside his own discourse in answer to a question about why some saints are remembered and others are not
stops.campa: Someone in the assembly asks why some saints are famous and others vanish. The master does not answer in his own voice. He quotes Hamid ad-din Suwali of Nagaur, a Chishti of the generation before his own, and the sentence is spoken by a man sitting in a village hut outside a capital he will not enter, to a scribe who will make it permanent. Seven hundred years later the hamlet carries his name, and the sultans who summoned him are read chiefly through his refusals.
stops.quote: He who strives to become famous during his lifetime—after he dies his name will be forgotten, while he who conceals his identity during his lifetime—after he dies his name will resound throughout the world!
stops.quote_source: Hamid ad-din Suwali of Nagaur, quoted by Nizam ad-Din in Fawa'id al-Fu'ad / Morals for the Heart, trans. Bruce B. Lawrence, Fascicle I, Assembly 1, p. 82
suggested_refs: Hamid ad-din Suwali of Nagaur, Chishti contemporary of Bakhtiar Kaki
sources: Fawa'id al-Fu'ad, trans. Lawrence, p. 82 (verified; the pool cited p. 81)

stops.name: Ghiyaspur, the man who flew over the khanqah
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, same assembly. The story is one Nizam ad-Din tells about Shaykh Abd al-Qadir Jilani of Baghdad; the speaker inside the anecdote is Jilani, and the quotation as it stands in the pool is an ellipsis-joined composite of a dialogue
stops.campa: He tells his circle a story about Abd al-Qadir Jilani of Baghdad, the founder whose order Abdelkader's family will keep six centuries later in Algeria. A man passes above the hospice through the air and does not trouble to go around it, and Jilani, informed of the flight, is annoyed about the manners rather than impressed by the flying. The man drops. The lesson is not that a saint could fly. The lesson is that flying is no excuse for going over someone's roof.
stops.quote: Fie! He has been disrespectful ... he is one of God's deputies. Day before yesterday he, together with two of his companions, were winging through the air.
stops.quote_source: Shaykh Abd al-Qadir Jilani, in an anecdote told by Nizam ad-Din; Fawa'id al-Fu'ad / Morals for the Heart, trans. Bruce B. Lawrence, Fascicle I, Assembly 1, p. 82 (composite of a dialogue, joined by ellipsis)
suggested_refs: The Qadiriyya of Baghdad and its reputation in fourteenth-century Delhi
sources: Fawa'id al-Fu'ad, trans. Lawrence, p. 82 (verified; the pool cited p. 81)

stops.name: Ghiyaspur, the second assembly and the freed slave
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: 8 Sha'ban 707 AH, 4 February 1308
stops.campa: Malih, a slave whom Amir Hasan Sijzi has freed, takes the oath of discipleship. The master marks the occasion with a sentence that removes the category rather than softening it. It is said in a sultanate whose ruling houses trace themselves to slave soldiers, in a decade when the throne changes hands by murder, to a room containing a scribe, a poet, and a man who was property last week. The scribe writes it down, dates it to the eighth of Sha'ban, and does not comment.
stops.quote: THERE IS NO SUCH THING AS SLAVERY AND DOMINION IN THE WAY; all who enter properly into the world of love do God's work.
stops.quote_source: Fawa'id al-Fu'ad / Morals for the Heart, trans. Bruce B. Lawrence, Fascicle I, Assembly 2, 8 Sha'ban 707 AH / 4 February 1308, p. 83
suggested_refs: The oath of discipleship at the Ghiyaspur khanqah
sources: Fawa'id al-Fu'ad, trans. Lawrence, p. 83 (verified against the archive.org djvu-text scan)

stops.name: Ghiyaspur, the fifth assembly and the exertion required
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: Friday 5 Ramadan 707 AH, 2 March 1308; assembly header verified in the scan
stops.campa: On the fifth of Ramadan, with the khanqah fasting, he takes up the oldest problem in the discipline: whether a man arrives by grace or by effort, and what is left of effort once grace is admitted. He does not choose a side. He affirms the grace and then leaves the obligation standing anyway, unrelieved, in the same breath. The book keeps that register throughout, and nobody in the room is let off the walking on the grounds that the walking was never theirs to begin with.
stops.quote: Whoever achieves his objective through virtuous action is the beneficiary of divine grace ... yet it is still incumbent on man to exert himself!
stops.quote_source: Fawa'id al-Fu'ad / Morals for the Heart, trans. Bruce B. Lawrence, Fascicle I, Assembly 5, Friday 5 Ramadan 707 AH / 2 March 1308, p. 87
suggested_refs: The Ramadan assemblies of 707 AH at Ghiyaspur
sources: Fawa'id al-Fu'ad, trans. Lawrence, p. 87 (verified; the pool cited p. 86)

stops.name: Ghiyaspur, the sixth assembly and the loin cloth
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: Friday 5 Shawwal 707 AH, 30 March 1308
stops.campa: Asked what renouncing the world means, he refuses the picture everyone brings to the question. Not nakedness, not a loin cloth, not a cave. Clothes and food, used up as they come to hand, with nothing put by and nothing held on to. He is saying this in a hospice that feeds anyone who arrives and keeps no stores, four miles from a treasury. In the same assembly he passes on the rule Khwaja Ajall Shirazi gave a new disciple: wish for yourself only what you also wish for others.
stops.quote: Renouncing worldliness does not mean, for instance, that one becomes naked, wearing only a loin cloth and sitting in solitude. Renouncing worldliness means, instead, to wear clothes and to take food while at the same time keeping in continuous use whatever comes to hand, feeling no inclination to hoard and no attachment to material objects.
stops.quote_source: Fawa'id al-Fu'ad / Morals for the Heart, trans. Bruce B. Lawrence, Fascicle I, Assembly 6, 5 Shawwal 707 AH / 30 March 1308, p. 88
suggested_refs: Khwaja Ajall Shirazi, whose rule of reciprocity Nizam ad-Din retells in the same assembly, p. 88
sources: Fawa'id al-Fu'ad, trans. Lawrence, p. 88 (verified against the archive.org djvu-text scan)

stops.name: Delhi, the court he never enters
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from secondary accounts across Alauddin Khalji's reign, 1296-1316; no court record has been read, and the year is a placeholder mid-reign
stops.campa: Through twenty years of Alauddin Khalji, the sultan who beats back the Mongols and fixes the price of grain by decree, Nizam ad-Din never appears at court and never receives a sultan at the khanqah in person. No source places him at a Khalji court site, and the absence is the evidence. Later Chishti tradition makes the stance doctrine: a shaikh who takes a stipend takes an owner. The distance is four miles and it is maintained in both directions for two decades without a single recorded meeting.
suggested_refs: The Chishti principle of refusing state patronage, formulated against the Khalji court
sources: general consensus across the biographies consulted

stops.name: Ghiyaspur, the Jamat Khana Masjid
stops.date_confidence: attested: completion between 1312 and 1313 under Alauddin Khalji, built by his son Khizr Khan. The pool's alternative window of 1315-1325 is impossible, since Khizr Khan was imprisoned and blinded in 1316
stops.campa: Khizr Khan, eldest son of Alauddin Khalji, raises a red sandstone mosque of three bays inside the khanqah precinct, finished by 1313. The sultan's own heir builds for the shaikh his father's court keeps at arm's length. Four years later Khizr Khan is imprisoned and blinded, and the throne passes to a brother who will threaten the same shaikh with an executive order. The mosque stands through all of it and is standing now, the oldest thing at the site.
suggested_refs: The Jamat Khana Masjid at Nizamuddin, red sandstone, completed 1312-1313

stops.name: Ghiyaspur, the six hundred deputies
stops.date_confidence: attested in substance: Wikipedia cites over six hundred khalifas authorized across his lifetime. The year is a placeholder late in that lifetime, not a documented date
stops.campa: Over his life he authorizes more than six hundred khalifas and sends them out with ijaza to teach. They go to Bengal, to the Deccan, to Gujarat, to Punjab, and the branch they carry is called Chishti Nizami after him. He has built no fortress, commanded no army, and never drawn a salary from anyone's treasury. The instrument of transmission is a man given permission and told to leave, and on that alone the order outlives every dynasty that shares its century.
suggested_refs: The Chishti Nizami branch and its diffusion across the subcontinent

stops.name: Ghiyaspur, the summons of Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah
stops.date_confidence: the Masjid-i Miri and the refusal are attested verbatim; the year is a placeholder inside the reign of 14 April 1316 to July 1320. Two details attached to this in the pool, a ban on nobles visiting Ghiyaspur and a delegate sent in his place, appear in neither article and are dropped
stops.campa: Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah builds the Masjid-i Miri and orders every Sufi and alim in Delhi to pray in it. Nizam ad-Din refuses, arguing that the mosque in his own neighborhood has the greater claim on him. It is a lawyer's answer from a man trained at Badaun in exactly the discipline required to make it. The sultan escalates: if the shaikh does not attend him in person at the start of the next lunar month, attendance will be compelled by executive order.
suggested_refs: The Masjid-i Miri of Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah, built to compel the attendance of the Delhi ulama

stops.name: Ghiyaspur, the prayer at the mother's tomb
stops.date_confidence: attested verbatim as an event. Date corrected from the pool's 1319 to 1320: the ultimatum named the start of the next lunar month and the sultan died on 1 Jumada II, so the confrontation falls in the weeks before the July 1320 assassination. The month is inferred, not stated
stops.campa: The deadline stands and the shaikh does not go. He walks to his mother's grave, prays there, and walks back to his jama'at-khana. That is the whole of the recorded response to a sovereign's threat: a son visiting a woman who brought him from Badaun to Delhi with nothing, seventy-five years earlier. He does not preach against the sultan, publish a refusal, or leave the city. He goes to the grave and comes home, and the throne does not survive the month.
suggested_refs: The tomb of Bibi Zulekha near Ghiyaspur, and the jama'at-khana he returned to
sources: Wikipedia, 'Nizamuddin Auliya' (quoted verbatim: 'the Shaikh quietly prayed at his mother's tomb and returned to his jama'at-khana')

stops.name: Delhi, the sultan cut down in his palace
stops.date_confidence: contradiction between two Wikipedia articles, unresolved: 'Nizamuddin Auliya' gives 8 July 1320, 'Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah' gives 9 July 1320, murdered and beheaded by Khusrau Khan in a palace revolt
stops.campa: Khusrau Khan kills Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah in the palace and has him beheaded. The reign that ordered Delhi's Sufis into a state mosque lasts four years and three months. The shaikh who declined the order is not implicated, not questioned, and not moved; he is where he has been since 1266. The two articles that record the killing cannot agree on whether it falls on the eighth of July or the ninth, which is a fair measure of how much of this century is documented and how much is remembered.
suggested_refs: The palace revolt of Khusrau Khan, July 1320, ending the Khalji dynasty

stops.name: Delhi, Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq takes the throne
stops.date_confidence: attested that Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq founds the dynasty in 1320; the month is inferred from the sequence after the July revolt. Wikipedia describes the relationship with Nizam ad-Din as initially cordial and later spoiled by 'opinion disharmony', with no documentary specifics
stops.campa: Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq puts down Khusrau Khan and founds the third dynasty of the sultanate. He is the fifth sultan Nizam ad-Din has outlasted in one village. The relationship starts cordial. Wikipedia's phrase for what happens to it is opinion disharmony, offered without a single documented particular, which is an honest way of saying that the sources record a quarrel and not its cause. Everything else the legend supplies about the quarrel was supplied afterward, by people who knew how it ended.
suggested_refs: The accession of Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq, September 1320

stops.name: Ghiyaspur, the baoli finished
stops.date_confidence: the completion of the stepwell in 1321 is attested; every story attached to it is not. Month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: The stepwell at the khanqah is finished in 1321, and it still holds water. Around it grows the most repeated legend in Delhi: that Ghiyasuddin forbade the laborers to work on it after hours so they would spend their days at Tughlaqabad, that he cut off their oil, and that the masons lit their lamps with water from the well after the shaikh blessed it. None of this is in a contemporary source. The stepwell is in the ground and the story is in the air, and the two have been inseparable for seven centuries.
suggested_refs: The baoli at Nizamuddin, completed 1321, still filled from the Yamuna aquifer

stops.name: Tughlaqabad, the fortress and the curse
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction throughout. The fort is real and was abandoned in 1327, six years after its founding; the curse is popular tradition with no primary attestation. Coordinate corrected from the pool's 77.2818, which falls about two kilometres east of the walls
stops.campa: The sultan raises a fortress city on the rocky ground south of Delhi, thirteen gates and a wall of cyclopean stone. Tradition gives the shaikh the sentence that answers it: ya rahe ujar, ya base gujar, let it stand empty or let herdsmen live in it. Tughlaqabad is abandoned in 1327, six years after it is founded, and the herdsmen move in. No contemporary chronicle records the curse. The ruins record the outcome, and the outcome is what kept the curse alive.
suggested_refs: Tughlaqabad Fort, founded 1321, abandoned 1327
sources: homegrown.co.in, 'Unravelling the Legends of Delhi's Cursed Tughlaqabad Fort'

stops.name: Ghiyaspur, Delhi is still far off
stops.date_confidence: legend, and the standard modern authority rejects it. Khaliq Ahmad Nizami calls the Bengal message and the shaikh's alleged reply 'both highly improbable', and identifies the earliest carrier as Yahya Sirhindi's Tarikh-i Mubarak Shahi, not Siyar al-Awliya and not Barani
stops.campa: The sultan is marching back from Bengal, and the message that reaches Ghiyaspur is said to order the shaikh out of Delhi before the royal party arrives. The answer he is said to give is four words long and is the most famous sentence he is ever recorded to have spoken. Nizami, editing the man's own recorded discourses six hundred years later, calls both the message and the reply highly improbable, and traces the line no further back than a fifteenth-century chronicle. It is kept here as legend, with the rejection on the face of it, because Delhi has gone on saying it for six centuries regardless.
stops.quote: Hunuz Dilli door ast (Delhi is still far).
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Nizam ad-Din Auliya, c. 1325; earliest carrier Yahya Sirhindi, Tarikh-i Mubarak Shahi, p. 96, per Khaliq Ahmad Nizami, Introduction to Morals for the Heart, Paulist Press 1992, p. 37 and n. 145, where Nizami rejects the episode as improbable
suggested_refs: Yahya Sirhindi, Tarikh-i Mubarak Shahi, earliest source for the saying (not fetched)
sources: Khaliq Ahmad Nizami, Introduction to Morals for the Heart, p. 37 and n. 145

stops.name: Afghanpur, the pavilion falls
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: 1 February 1325, confirmed by Muhammad bin Tughluq's accession on 4 February, 'three days after the death of his father'. Place is contested: the Wikipedia infobox says Kara-Manikpur, the standard Ibn Battuta-derived account says Afghanpur near Delhi
stops.campa: A wooden reception pavilion built to receive the returning sultan collapses on him and on his son Prince Mahmud Khan. He is dead on the first of February and his son Jauna Khan takes the throne on the fourth. Ibn Battuta, who will sit as qadi of this city nine years later, records the allegation that Jauna Khan engineered the collapse. The legend reads it as the shaikh's sentence coming true. The shaikh outlives him by two months, not by days, whatever the retellings say.
suggested_refs: Ibn Battuta's account of the Afghanpur pavilion and the accusation against Jauna Khan

stops.name: Ghiyaspur, death on the eighteenth of Rabi al-Thani
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, and the Hijri conversion checks: 3 April 1325 CE equals 18 Rabi al-Thani 725 AH, aged eighty-six or eighty-seven. The pool's alternative of 12 Rabi al-Awwal 725 AH converts to about 27 February and is wrong
stops.campa: He dies on the morning of the third of April, at the khanqah, eighty-six or eighty-seven years old, having lived fifty-nine of them in this one village. Seven sultans have held Delhi since he arrived in it. He never took a stipend, never entered a court, never made the hajj, and never travelled further than the Sutlej in one direction and the Ganges plain in the other. The record of what he actually said fills one book, written by a man who sat in the room and dated every entry.
suggested_refs: The jama'at-khana at Ghiyaspur where he died, 3 April 1325

stops.name: Nizamuddin, buried where the hut stood
stops.date_confidence: attested. The village of Ghiyaspur is renamed after him; who first built over the grave is contested, see the following stops
stops.campa: He is buried at the khanqah, on the ground he was sent to by a name spoken in a garden sixty years earlier. The village stops being Ghiyaspur and becomes Nizamuddin, which is what it is called today, and the four miles between this grave and Bakhtiar Kaki's at Mehrauli become the axis of Chishti Delhi. Moinuddin Chishti sent Kaki to hold this city in 1214. The holding passes here, through Baba Farid and a turban carried down the Sutlej, and the anchor moves east across the ridge.
suggested_refs: The renaming of Ghiyaspur to Nizamuddin after the burial
sources: moinuddin_chishti.journey.json, stop 'Delhi, Mehrauli, the death of Bakhtiar Kaki'

stops.name: Nizamuddin, Amir Khusrow tears his clothes
stops.date_confidence: tradition, hagiographic rather than documentary; the day is inferred from accounts that put him away from Delhi at the death and arriving immediately after
stops.campa: Amir Khusrow is out of the city when the death comes. The accounts say he tears his clothes, covers himself in dust, and does not recover. He has served seven sultans as a court poet and written in two languages, and none of that is what the tradition remembers about him. What it remembers is a man sitting at a grave in Ghiyaspur for six months and then dying. The framing is poetic rather than documentary, it rests on later hagiography, and no source consulted contradicts it.
suggested_refs: The Persian and Hindavi laments attributed to Amir Khusrow on his master's death

stops.name: Delhi, Nasiruddin Mahmud takes the succession
stops.date_confidence: attested that Nasiruddin Mahmud, Chiragh-e-Dehli, is the designated successor and the last of the great early Delhi Chishtis; the month is inferred, not documented
stops.campa: Nasiruddin Mahmud, called Chiragh-e-Dehli, the lamp of Delhi, takes the succession. He is counted the fifth and last of the great early Chishti masters of the Delhi line, which begins at Ajmer with Moinuddin, comes to Mehrauli with Bakhtiar Kaki, goes up the Sutlej to Baba Farid, comes back to Ghiyaspur, and stops here. After him the order does not lack shaikhs. It lacks a single centre, because six hundred deputies have already been sent out to be centres elsewhere.
suggested_refs: The dargah of Nasiruddin Chiragh Dehlavi at Chirag Delhi

stops.name: Nizamuddin, Khusrow buried at his master's feet
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month: Amir Khusrow dies in October 1325, within about six months of his master, and is buried at his feet in the same complex. Day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Khusrow dies in October, six months behind him, and is buried at the entrance to the complex, at his master's feet, which is where he had asked to be. The saying about the same grave is recorded on the master's side, with the legal impediment named in the same breath as the wish. Two urs are kept at this one site every year, his on 17 and 18 Rabi al-Thani and Khusrow's on 18 Shawwal, and the qawwals who sing at both sing verses written by the man in the smaller tomb.
stops.quote: If the sharia allowed me I would have liked him to be buried with me in the same grave.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Nizam ad-Din Auliya concerning Amir Khusrow; Wikipedia, 'Nizamuddin Auliya'; Google Arts and Culture entry on Amir Khusrow
suggested_refs: The tomb of Amir Khusrow at the entrance of the Nizamuddin Dargah complex

stops.name: Nizamuddin, Muhammad bin Tughlaq builds over the grave
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, unresolved. Wikipedia 'Nizamuddin Dargah' and tourmyindia.com credit Muhammad bin Tughlaq with the main structure in 1325, immediately after the death; Wikipedia 'Nizamuddin Auliya' dates the standing shrine structure to 1562. Both are carried
stops.campa: The sultan whose father died under a collapsing pavilion, and whom Ibn Battuta accuses of building it, is recorded as a follower of the shaikh and as the man who first raised a structure over the grave. He also adds two flanking domed halls to Khizr Khan's mosque. Whether the shrine as it now stands is his or belongs to 1562 is a straight contradiction between two articles about the same site, and it is left standing here rather than smoothed away.
suggested_refs: The domed halls flanking the Jamat Khana Masjid, added c. 1325
sources: Wikipedia, 'Nizamuddin Auliya' (which dates the structure to 1562)

stops.name: Delhi, Ibn Battuta takes the qadi's seat
stops.date_confidence: attested that Ibn Battuta serves as qadi of Delhi under Muhammad bin Tughluq for roughly seven or eight years from about 1334; whether he ever visited this dargah is not stated in any atlas file and the Rihla was not checked for it here
stops.campa: Nine years after the burial, Ibn Battuta arrives from Morocco and is made qadi of Delhi under the sultan who buried Ghiyasuddin. By his time the order Moinuddin Chishti planted generations earlier has become the establishment, and the Chishti shrines are the ones the sultans go to. That establishment is four miles east of the qadi's court, under a dome raised nine years before he got there, and it is this man's doing.
suggested_refs: The Rihla of Ibn Battuta, on the Delhi of Muhammad bin Tughluq

stops.name: Nizamuddin, Amir Khwurd writes the Siyar al-Awliya
stops.date_confidence: attested in substance: Amir Khwurd, Sayyid Muhammad Mubarak Kirmani, a disciple distinct from Amir Khusrow, completes the compendium around the 1360s. Exact year not fixed; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Amir Khwurd, a disciple of this khanqah, writes the Siyar al-Awliya, the biographical compendium of the Chishti masters, decades after the death. It becomes the source that later hands quote when they cannot quote a document, cited for lineage claims stretching back centuries before its own author was born, an 1884 Delhi reprint still doing that work four hundred years further on. The book outlives the room it was written in by longer than the order itself had then existed.
suggested_refs: Amir Khwurd, Siyar al-Awliya, and its 1884 Delhi reprint

stops.name: Nizamuddin, the book that outweighed a divan
stops.date_confidence: the reception of the Fawa'id al-Fu'ad among later mystics is reported by the modern editor without a date; the year is a placeholder in the generation after the death. Firuz Shah Tughlaq's repair of the dargah is likewise attested without a year
stops.campa: Firuz Shah Tughlaq repairs the shrine and hangs four golden cups from the recesses of its dome. In the same generation the book Amir Hasan Sijzi kept is being read past exhaustion, and the offer Khusrow is said to have made for it is preserved by a modern editor rather than by a medieval one. Two poets served this khanqah. One of them wrote the divans that made Persian poetry in India, and is remembered for offering to trade them all for the notes the other one took.
stops.quote: While mystics like Maulana 'Ala ad-din Nili kept themselves busy in reading it, Amir Khusrau, the famous poet, offered to exchange all his works for it.
stops.quote_source: Khaliq Ahmad Nizami, Introduction to Morals for the Heart, Paulist Press 1992, p. 4; this is the modern editor's prose about the book's reception, not a saying of either man
suggested_refs: The four golden cups suspended from the dome by Firuz Shah Tughlaq
sources: Khaliq Ahmad Nizami, Introduction to Morals for the Heart, p. 4 (verified; the pool cited p. 24 and credited Lawrence)

stops.name: Nizamuddin, the marble dome of Faridun Khan
stops.date_confidence: attested: the present marble dome, roughly six metres across, is built by Faridun Khan in 1562 under Akbar. Month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Faridun Khan raises the marble dome that pilgrims see now, six metres across, in the fourth year of Akbar's reign. It is Mughal work over a Tughlaq grave, and it is the reason one source dates the standing shrine to 1562 while another dates it to 1325. Both are describing the same building at different depths. In the same century the Mughals begin burying their own inside the precinct, which is how a hut on the Yamuna acquires an emperor's daughter for a neighbour.
suggested_refs: The marble dome of 1562 over the tomb of Nizam ad-Din Auliya

stops.name: Nizamuddin Basti, the graves that gather
stops.date_confidence: attested that Jahanara Begum, the emperor Muhammad Shah, and more than seventy others are buried within the complex; Jahanara died in 1681 and the year is taken from her burial. Ghalib's grave nearby, in the Loharu family plot, is a later addition
stops.campa: More than seventy people are buried inside the complex, among them Jahanara Begum, daughter of Shah Jahan, who chose an open grave under the sky here rather than a mausoleum, and the emperor Muhammad Shah. Mirza Ghalib lies a short walk away in the Loharu family plot, his tomb restored by the Aga Khan Trust for Culture with the Archaeological Survey of India in 2009. The precinct keeps drawing what it drew when there was nothing there but a kitchen: people who would rather be near this than near a throne.
suggested_refs: The open-air grave of Jahanara Begum in the Nizamuddin precinct; the tomb of Mirza Ghalib in Nizamuddin Basti

stops.name: Nizamuddin Basti, the urs and the qawwals
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the award: UNESCO Asia-Pacific Awards for Excellence and Sustainable Development, 1 December 2021, following a public-private partnership signed 11 July 2007. The urs dates, 17-18 Rabi al-Thani and 18 Shawwal, are attested and recur annually
stops.campa: The urs is kept every year on the seventeenth and eighteenth of Rabi al-Thani, and Khusrow's on the eighteenth of Shawwal, and qawwali is sung at the tomb nightly by singers working in a form the tradition credits to the man buried at the feet of the man in the dome. The Aga Khan Trust for Culture, the Archaeological Survey, and the Delhi civic bodies conserve sixty monuments and two hundred acres around the basti and take a UNESCO award for it. Pilgrims of every faith come all year, as they did when the kitchen was open.
suggested_refs: The Nizamuddin Urban Renewal Initiative, 2007 onward, and the UNESCO Asia-Pacific Awards of 1 December 2021
